sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) is the discipline of treating operations as a software engineering problem — using error budgets, SLOs, SLIs, toil reduction, blameless postmortems, and data-driven capacity planning to make large systems reliable without scaling human toil linearly with traffic.
Site Reliability Engineering originated at Google in 2003 when Ben Treynor Sloss was asked to run the production operations team and chose to staff it with software engineers rather than traditional sysadmins. The founding insight was that operations, when treated as a manual craft, scales linearly with the number of services and the volume of traffic — every new microservice needs another human carrying a pager, every new region needs another ops team, every new failure mode needs another runbook update. SRE flips this by applying software engineering techniques (automation, version control, design review, postmortems) to the operation of systems, with the explicit goal of capping operational toil at 50% of each engineer's time and spending the other 50% building durable engineering improvements. The result, documented in the 2016 *Site Reliability Engineering* book and refined across Google's two-decade history, is a methodology that lets a few hundred engineers run services serving billions of users with measurable reliability.

The first foundational concept is the SLI/SLO/SLA hierarchy. An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a quantitative measure of service health — typically the ratio of good events to total events, such as "the fraction of HTTP requests that returned in under 400 ms with a 2xx status." An SLO (Service Level Objective) is the target value for that SLI over a window — "99.9% of requests succeed over a rolling 30-day window." An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is the contractual version, set lower than the SLO (e.g., 99.5%) and accompanied by financial penalties if breached, giving the team a safety margin between internal target and customer-visible promise. Google's rule of thumb is that the SLA should sit one 9 below the SLO so that internal SLO misses are not automatically customer-facing breaches. The discipline is to define SLIs that capture user experience (latency at p99, not average; success as user-visible outcome, not HTTP 2xx), because an SLO on the wrong SLI is worse than no SLO at all.

The second concept is the error budget, the most operationally consequential SRE idea. If the SLO is 99.9% availability over 30 days, the system is allowed 43.2 minutes of unavailability per month — that is the error budget. The budget is a shared resource between product and engineering: as long as budget remains, product can ship features, push risky migrations, and freeze infrastructure for deploy windows; once the budget is exhausted, engineering gets to gate all further changes behind reliability work until the budget recovers. This converts the previously political argument ("when can we ship?") into a quantitative one ("do we have budget?") and aligns product and reliability incentives without top-down mandates. Google's own experience is that error budgets reduce unplanned downtime by forcing teams to slow down when reliability slips, and they make freeze periods self-enforcing rather than requiring executive edict.

The third concept is toil reduction. Toil is operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly with service growth. Restarting a crashed pod, hand-filling a capacity request ticket, copying log lines into a postmortem, manually rotating certificates — these are toil. SRE's hard rule is that toil must be capped at 50% of each engineer's time; if it exceeds 50% for two consecutive quarters, the team has a staffing or automation problem that must be addressed before any new feature work is taken on. The remedy is to systematically automate the highest-toil task each sprint, replacing it with code (a controller, a script, a runbook automation) that performs the task deterministically. Over quarters this compounds: the team that automates one task per sprint has, after a year, eliminated 26 toil items and built a library of reusable automation. Netflix's engineering culture formalizes this as "build toil-free platforms" — the goal is not to automate existing toil but to redesign the platform so the toil cannot exist.

The fourth concept is the blameless postmortem, addressed in detail in Topic 7 but central to SRE culture. The rule is that the engineer who triggered an incident is the most important person in the postmortem room, because they know more about what happened than anyone else, and the assumption is that they did what any reasonable engineer would have done given the information and tools they had. The fault is in the system — the deploy process, the access controls, the test coverage — not the engineer. Blameful postmortems cause engineers to hide future incidents, which prevents learning, which guarantees recurrence. Google, Netflix, and the broader SRE community treat blamelessness as a non-negotiable engineering value, and postmortems are published broadly internally so that other teams can learn from the same mistakes without re-committing them.

The fifth concept is capacity planning. SRE treats capacity as a forecasting problem: traffic grows at a known rate (often tied to product forecasts), each service has a known per-request cost (CPU, memory, network), and the headroom required to survive a single-region failure is known (typically N+1 or N+2). The capacity plan projects these forward 6–12 months and converts them into a procurement plan — when to order servers, when to provision new clusters, when to add CDN capacity. The discipline is to plan for peak × (1 + margin) and to re-forecast monthly, because forecasts based on last month's traffic systematically under-provision during growth periods. Google's capacity planning for Search, described in the SRE book, uses Monte Carlo simulation over traffic distributions and failure modes to produce probabilistic headroom targets; most teams use simpler deterministic models, but the principle — capacity is forecastable, not reactive — is universal.

The sixth concept is change management. SRE's posture is that changes (deploys, config edits, migrations) are the single largest source of incidents — Google's data shows roughly 70% of outages are caused by changes, not by capacity or dependency failures. The mitigations are progressive rollout (canary, then 1%, then 10%, then 100%), reversible changes (every deploy must have a one-command rollback), and batched changes (never change code and config simultaneously, so a regression's cause is unambiguous). Microsoft's Azure SRE organization formalizes this as "Safe Deployment": ring-based rollout (ring 0 = team, ring 1 = internal, ring 2 = early adopters, ring 3 = production), automated rollback on error-rate threshold, and a requirement that every change be reproducible from source. Netflix's "Chap" deployment system and the broader "progressive delivery" movement (Flagger, Argo Rollouts, Spinnaker) all encode the same principle: ship small, ship slowly, ship reversibly.

The trade-off in SRE is reliability versus velocity. Pure reliability work — long freezes, exhaustive testing, conservative capacity — slows product velocity to a crawl; pure velocity work — uncontrolled deploys, no error budgets — produces outages that themselves destroy velocity (the team spends a week firefighting instead of building). The SRE answer is the error budget: it explicitly quantifies the trade-off and lets the team spend budget on velocity when reliability is high and reclaim budget for reliability work when it slips. This turns a previously political argument into a measured one, and it is the deepest contribution of SRE to operations engineering.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[SLI: e.g. % requests < 400ms] --> B[SLO: 99.9% over 30d]
    B --> C[Error Budget: 43.2 min/month]
    C --> D{Budget remaining?}
    D -- yes --> E[Ship features, run migrations]
    D -- no --> F[Freeze changes, pay down toil]
    E --> G[Monitor burn rate]
    F --> G
    G --> H{Burn rate > 14x?}
    H -- yes --> I[Page on-call immediately]
    H -- no --> J{Burn rate > 6x over 1h?}
    J -- yes --> K[Ticket: investigate]
    J -- no --> L[Continue]
    K --> M[Blameless postmortem]
    I --> M
    M --> N[Action items + owners]
    N --> O[Capacity plan revised]
    O --> A
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
  SLI   =  good_events / total_events
   |
   v
  +----------+    target     +----------+
  |   SLI    | ------------> |   SLO    |  99.9% / 30d
  +----------+               +----------+
                                  |
                                  | 100% - SLO
                                  v
                          +----------------+
                          | Error Budget   |  43.2 min/mo
                          +----------------+
                                  |
                  +---------------+---------------+
                  |                               |
            budget left                       budget spent
                  |                               |
                  v                               v
          +---------------+              +-----------------+
          | ship features |              | freeze changes  |
          | run migrations|              | pay down toil   |
          +---------------+              | write postmortem|
                  |                     +-----------------+
                  |                               |
                  +------- burn-rate alert --------+
                                  |
                                  v
                      +-------------------------+
                      | Blameless postmortem    |
                      |  -> action items        |
                      |  -> capacity re-forecast|
                      +-------------------------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. The team defines an SLI that captures user-visible health (e.g., fraction of requests that returned in under 400 ms with 2xx status) and an SLO target (e.g., 99.9% over a rolling 30-day window).
2. The error budget is computed as `(1 - SLO) × window`: for 99.9% over 30 days, that is 43.2 minutes of allowed unavailability per month.
3. As long as budget remains, product can ship features and engineering can run migrations; once the budget is exhausted, all changes are frozen until reliability work restores headroom.
4. Burn-rate alerts fire when the budget is being consumed too fast — 14× burn pages immediately (a 2% budget drain in 1 hour means an SLO breach in 5 hours), 6× over 1 hour opens a ticket.
5. After any incident, a blameless postmortem produces action items with owners and feeds back into the capacity plan for the next forecast cycle.

quiz.explanation: A useful SLI captures user-visible service health directly. The canonical recipe is "the ratio of good events to total events, where good is defined by what the user experiences as success." For an HTTP API, that means counting as good only requests that returned a 2xx status within a latency threshold (say, 400 ms at p99) — not all 2xx regardless of latency, and not average latency.
